title: What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules
summary: **Reverse engineering** means working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. It is how security researchers find vulnerabilities, how malware is analysed, how old software is kept running and how file formats are documented for interoperability. This lesson sets out what it involves, the tools, and the legal and ethical ground rules this course follows.
markdown:
## Running the pipeline backwards Lesson 1.04's pipeline turned source into machine code. Reverse engineering goes the other way, recovering understanding, never the original source, from the compiled program: ```mermaid flowchart RL E["game.exe
bytes"] --> P["Parse the file format
(PE: lessons 9.02, 9.03)"] P --> D["Disassemble
machine code to assembly (ch. 7)"] D --> S["Recover structure
functions, loops, classes (9.05, 9.06)"] S --> M["Understand meaning
names, types, intent (9.08, 9.09)"] ``` The earlier chapters were the preparation: the PE format of chapter 6's modules, the assembly of chapter 7, the debuggers of chapters 4 and 8, and the layouts of chapters 2 and 3. ## Who does it, and why | Field | What they reverse engineer | |---|---| | **Security research** | Software, to find and responsibly report vulnerabilities before attackers do | | **Malware analysis** | Malicious programs, to understand them, detect them and remove them | | **Interoperability** | File formats and protocols, so that other programs can read and write them (many open-source tools exist because of this) | | **Preservation and compatibility** | Old software and games whose source is lost, to keep them running on new systems | | **Debugging and support** | Third-party libraries and drivers without source, when they misbehave inside your program | | **Learning** | How compilers, operating systems and well-written programs work | ## Static and dynamic analysis - **Static analysis** examines the program without running it: reading the file's headers and the disassembly, following cross-references (lessons 9.02 to 9.06, 9.08). Tools: Ghidra, IDA, Binary Ninja, `dumpbin`. - **Dynamic analysis** runs it and watches: breakpoints, memory, calls into the operating system (lesson 9.07). Tools: x64dbg, WinDbg, Visual Studio, Process Monitor. Each answers what the other cannot. Static analysis sees every path, including ones that rarely run; dynamic analysis sees real values and resolves indirect calls. Real work alternates between them. ## The ground rules for this course Reverse engineering is a legitimate, widely practised skill. Like any capability, how it is used matters, and the law varies by country. The rules this course follows: 1. **Practise on programs you have the right to analyse**: programs you compiled yourself (lesson 9.10 builds a series of practice targets), open-source programs (where you can check your conclusions against the source), and challenges published specifically as practice ("crackmes" and capture-the-flag tasks). 2. **Read the licence.** Many licences restrict reverse engineering. Some laws allow limited reverse engineering for specific purposes such as interoperability (for example, Article 6 of the EU Software Directive) or good-faith security research, with conditions. When it matters, ask someone qualified rather than assuming. 3. **Do not use it to cheat other people.** Altering online games to gain an advantage over other players, or bypassing anti-cheat systems, harms those players, breaks the terms you agreed to and can break the law. This course does not teach that, and it does not teach defeating copy protection or licence checks. 4. **Report vulnerabilities responsibly.** If you find a security flaw, tell the vendor privately, through their security contact or bug bounty programme, and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly. 5. **Handle malware with care.** Real malicious samples belong in an isolated virtual machine with no access to your files or network, which lesson 15.08 sets up. The practice targets in this course are harmless programs you build yourself. ## What you can expect to recover | Survives compilation | Lost | |---|---| | The machine code and its control flow | Comments, formatting, local variable names | | String literals and constants | Most type information (structs become offsets, lesson 7.08) | | Imported and exported function names | Templates and inline functions as separate entities | | Class names (through RTTI, lesson 9.06), if not disabled | Macros, `constexpr` values folded into code | | Everything, if a PDB is available | The original structure of the source files | Recovering a program's logic is slow, careful work, done function by function. Recovering its exact source is impossible. Good reverse engineers are patient, take notes, and name things as they understand them. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Starting with a large, unfamiliar program > Practise on small programs you wrote, where you can check every conclusion against the source. > [!warning] Trusting the decompiler blindly > Decompiler output is a guess at C code. Check important conclusions against the assembly. > [!warning] Assuming that being able to do it means being allowed to > Check the licence and the law, and stay within the ground rules. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Name four legitimate uses of reverse engineering. - Copying a game's code into your own, removing licence checks, unlocking paid content, cheating online + Security research, malware analysis, interoperability with file formats and protocols, and preserving old software - Changing a program's author name, redistributing it, selling it, renaming it - Speeding up the compiler, shrinking source files, writing comments, formatting code > Debugging third-party code and learning are also legitimate. The ground rules of the course rule out piracy and cheating in online games. ? What do reverse engineers recover, and what can they not recover? + Logic, strings and imports, but not comments, local names or source - They recover the original source code exactly, but not the strings - They recover comments and local names, but not the control flow - They recover nothing useful without a PDB > Compiling throws away comments and local names for good; the behaviour remains in the machine code. ? What should you do if you find a security vulnerability? - Publish the details at once so users can protect themselves - Keep it secret and say nothing - Sell it to whoever offers the most + Report it privately to the vendor and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly > This is responsible disclosure: users get a fix before attackers learn the details. ? What is the difference between static and dynamic analysis? + Static examines the program unrun; dynamic runs and observes it - Static analysis is for small programs, dynamic for large ones - They are the same thing > Each reveals things the other cannot; real work uses both. ? Which of these is lost when a program is compiled without a PDB? - String literals - Imported function names + Local variable names > Locals become registers and stack offsets. ? Which practice targets does this course use? - Commercial online games you own - Anti-cheat software and its drivers + Programs you build yourself, and open source > These are targets you clearly have the right to analyse. ```
ideas:
- Pick a small open-source command-line tool, build it without symbols, and keep its source closed for now: later lessons will use it as a target you can check your work against.
- Look up the licence of a program you use every day and find what it says about reverse engineering.
- Find your country's rules on reverse engineering for interoperability.

cards.q: Name four legitimate uses of reverse engineering.
cards.a:
Security research, malware analysis, interoperability with file formats and protocols, and preserving old software

Debugging third-party code and learning are also legitimate. The ground rules of the course rule out piracy and cheating in online games.

cards.q: What do reverse engineers recover, and what can they not recover?
cards.a:
Logic, strings and imports, but not comments, local names or source

Compiling throws away comments and local names for good; the behaviour remains in the machine code.

cards.q: What should you do if you find a security vulnerability?
cards.a:
Report it privately to the vendor and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly

This is responsible disclosure: users get a fix before attackers learn the details.

cards.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic analysis?
cards.a:
Static examines the program unrun; dynamic runs and observes it

Each reveals things the other cannot; real work uses both.

cards.q: Which of these is lost when a program is compiled without a PDB?
cards.a:
Local variable names

Locals become registers and stack offsets.

cards.q: Which practice targets does this course use?
cards.a:
Programs you build yourself, and open source

These are targets you clearly have the right to analyse.
